title: Rich toward God (Luke 12:13–21)
hookLine: someone asks him to split an inheritance, and he warns against greed

cards: Jesus has just been talking about courage before judges and the Holy Spirit's help, and a voice from the crowd cuts right across it: "Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me."
You can almost hear the family behind it. A parent has died. Someone thinks they got less than their share.
There have been arguments at the kitchen table, and maybe nobody's speaking now. So the man brings it to the teacher everyone is listening to. Surely he'll take my side.

teach.b: The law of Moses had rules for how an inheritance was split, but Jesus won't do it: "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?"
He goes underneath the question: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."
The Greek word for covetousness is pleonexia, the itch for more.
Not wanting things, exactly; wanting more than. More than my brother. More than last year.
A rich man's land produces a huge harvest, and he has a conversation. Listen to who's in it. He thinks within himself.
I will pull down my barns, I will build greater. Then he talks to his own soul: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry."
No family, no neighbor, no worker who brought the harvest in, no God. Only him, his barns and his soul. That night, God speaks for the first time in the story and calls him a fool.
His life is required of him, and who will own it all now? Then the last line: "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God." Rich toward God.
Rich in a direction: wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns. And it loops back to the brothers.
An inheritance fight is exactly what the rich fool's barns could turn into.

how: Christians read the rich fool when thinking about money, wills and generosity; some churches teach tithing, giving a set share of income, and some Christians name charities in their wills as a way of being rich toward God.

o: a fair share of a family inheritance
the itch for more, wanting more than others
careful saving for the hard years ahead

p: wants his share of the inheritance
talks only to his own soul

s: Jesus settles the brothers' inheritance case
"man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" he goes underneath the question instead.
in the story, the rich man talks only to himself
he thinks within himself and speaks to his own soul. nobody else is in the conversation until God speaks.
Jesus says owning things is a sin
he warns against covetousness: a life doesn't consist in the abundance of things.

games.q: a man shouts from the crowd: master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. what does Jesus do?
o: he hears both brothers and decides the case.
he refuses to judge, and warns everyone about greed.
he tells the man to give his share away.
games.why: "who made me a judge or a divider over you?" then: "take heed, and beware of covetousness," and the story of the rich fool.

practice: Bring to mind a small disagreement you're carrying: whose turn it is to do the dishes, who owes whom for lunch, a borrowed thing never returned, a sibling squabble about something left behind.

Notice the part of you that keeps score, then imagine letting the score go, giving a little more than your share, and ask what that would really cost you. If you pray, ask for a heart that faces outward.

wordCard.voice: Pleonexia, Greek for covetousness, the itch for more: wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns and a conversation with only yourself.

orig.note: Greek: covetousness, greed, the urge for more. the King James Bible says covetousness.

carryVoice: Your line: treasure that faces outward. Rich, but in a direction. Day five hundred forty-eight.
